title: Memory-bounded systems and backpressure in Rust
body:
As everybody knows and especially nowadays with the RAM shortage situation because of LLMs, memory is not infinite. Therefore a lot of workloads, processes, pods need system limits. For instance in the case of embedded systems but also, more commonly in webservers, remote systems, and so on.
Indeed the machine hosting your process, be it virtual or physical won’t have infinite RAM and once it is exhausted, the kernel will slow down or kill processes through the OOM killer, which will degrade the service you are actually trying to provide.
For this reason, it is quite usual to add limits to processes or pods in a Kubernetes context, usually by using Linux cgroups, which are a way to add CPU and memory limits on processes. Today we will only talk about memory limits, CPU limits being a whole different topic.
So what do we mean by memory backpressure? Well this is simply the ability of a system to delay new workloads or slow down to limit its memory usage to a given threshold. There are multiple solutions depending on the programming language, the kind of system you are integrating this into and the architecture of your program. We will focus on Rust.
First, what can be bound and what cannot? The kernel enforces cgroup limits (memory.max) against everything charged to the cgroup, exposed as memory.current: the anonymous memory of its processes, the page cache of the files they read, write or memory-map, and kernel memory allocated on their behalf, such as socket buffers and page tables. Swap is accounted separately (memory.swap.max). When the limit is hit, the kernel first reclaims what it can, mostly clean page cache, and only then invokes the OOM killer. Kubernetes adds its own layer on top: when the node itself runs low on memory, the kubelet evicts pods, using their memory working set to rank them. The working set is memory.current minus the inactive, easily reclaimable file pages. A container exceeding its own limit is not evicted: it is killed by the kernel OOM killer.
The main focus here will be the process’s Resident Set Size (or RSS): the pages mapped by the process that are currently in RAM. It contains both reclaimable file-backed pages and anonymous memory. Only the latter is a problem: the kernel cannot drop it without swapping. A process RSS holds the following kinds of data:
The instructions of the program being run. These pages are backed by the executable file, so the kernel can drop them and read them back when needed.
The static sections: read-only data, also backed by the file, and mutable data (.data, .bss) which becomes anonymous memory once written.
Thread stacks: 2 MiB reserved per thread spawned with Rust’s std by default, and usually 8 MiB for the main thread. Only the pages actually touched count in RSS.
Resident pages of memory-mapped files, which are file-backed and reclaimable as well.
Memory allocated dynamically by the process through malloc: the heap.
The only manageable one is the memory allocated dynamically. The three following solutions will only concern this kind of memory and we will count the others as an overhead to measure, either constant or growing linearly with the load.
The three solutions will rely on these two known example systems:
A live ingestion HTTP server that is at the front of a data processing pipeline. We can picture this as a push based consumption model. Requests are pushed over the network, if it can’t accept traffic anymore, the server will reply a 503 status code with a Retry-After header.
A data processing system that will do CPU/Memory bound processing behind a stream implementation (Kafka/NATS). We can picture this as a pull based consumption model. The downstream service will pull new work to perform only when it can and will rely on the stream to act as a buffer in the meantime.
We can define this difference as cooperative backpressure vs. non-cooperative. Push based consumption model expects that the client respects the Retry-After header, but the client is not forced to. Pull based does not rely on an expected behavior.
Indirect memory bounding
This solution can be applied to any language. It is not specific to Rust.
The easiest way to bound your system memory is to limit two things:
The incoming load per request. For this we need to find a metric that scales linearly with the load of the service. For example with our server implementation it could be the request body size.
The maximum number of requests it can process in parallel with a semaphore.
If your system implements the tower Service trait (which I highly recommend for ecosystem integration purposes), you can leverage the concurrency limit layer for this and expose the concurrency limit as a configuration knob. If your memory allocation is tied to requests handling, this might be one of the easiest solutions.
Example: bounding an axum server with tower layers
Example: a bounded NATS JetStream pull consumer
Capacity planning and caveats
Once you have ways to limit the workload, you need to tune them and for this you need to measure the metrics you picked against the real memory usage and define a rule.
There are multiple caveats with this solution that will appear in this process:
You actually need to plan limits for the worst case scenario. For our server implementation, with a 5 MB request body and a concurrency limit set to 1000 requests in parallel, you will need to reserve up to 5 GB of memory. And actually most request bodies might only weigh 1 MB.
Other memory allocations, allocator overhead and memory fragmentation are not counted, so you need to account manually for them, and it might scale from inputs that are completely unrelated to the requests, like the number of CPU threads, the number of blocking threads spawned by tokio, the allocator used, the OS, and so on…
Byte-budget bounding
In fact, the capacity planning complexity and caveats come from the load per request; the maximum number of parallel requests itself being straightforward to plan.
So byte budget is another solution: bound the bytes a work task can hold, instead of the number of tasks.
The simplest byte budget is a semaphore with one permit per byte. Each request reserves its body size. With a 1 GiB budget, we still serve 1000 requests of 1 MiB in parallel, without reserving 5 GiB for the worst case.
Example: a byte budget for an axum server with a weighted semaphore
Be careful with compressed bodies: Content-Length is the compressed size, so the budget undercounts them. Our NATS consumer already had a byte budget: max_bytes_per_batch bounds the prefetch buffer in bytes.
You can go further and limit the allocated memory itself, either with a memory arena or a custom allocator.
One of its biggest advantages is that it allows for a finer customization of the system behavior while having a more precise idea of what we are limiting. And you can implement different behavior if your memory bound is reached, for example you can either flush processed data eagerly if it is a scratch bounded buffer of data or refuse any incoming data.
For a scratch buffer, bumpalo arenas have a set_allocation_limit. For a real-world example, look at DataFusion’s MemoryPool: operators reserve bytes before allocating, and spill to disk when the reservation fails.
However it might come with a heavier configuration burden as the operator needs to tweak multiple limits and understand how they interact with each other. Also it might not be applicable for every system.
Indeed, using such solutions might not be an option, especially if most of the allocations issued by your service are coming from external libs. Today, it is extremely rare to find crates that support custom allocators or that are only arena based. Some workloads cannot fit the bounded arena model and the allocator trait has only been stabilized in Rust 1.100. So far only Vec and Box support it.
Exploring global memory bounding
A lot of memory managed languages have ways of bounding memory globally through Garbage Collection with
a best-effort mechanism. Once a given threshold is reached, the GC starts to reclaim memory eagerly at the price of more pauses. Go has GOMEMLIMIT, Java has MaxRAMPercentage, … However there is no standard mechanism available for this in Rust (or any language that is not memory managed).
Still, you can use a custom allocator that will give you stats of your heap usage. These allocators are usually declared globally.
The most basic way is to make a custom wrapper to track allocated memory:
Example with a custom global allocator wrapper
However allocated memory is not the most representative metric and we can do much better!
Using Jemalloc
jemalloc is a general-purpose allocator originally written by Jason Evans for FreeBSD’s libc, and now maintained by Meta. It is one of the most feature-complete allocators, its performance is on par with the alternatives, and its main advantage for us is that it exposes a lot of memory usage statistics, which the tikv-jemalloc-ctl crate makes easy to read from Rust. This makes it a good fit for our use case: an HTTP server at the beginning of a data processing pipeline, ingesting and validating a high volume of data before it is processed downstream. Rust bindings and a ready to use crate are available with the tikv-jemallocator crate and maintained by the tikv organisation.
First step: collecting jemalloc metrics efficiently with OpenTelemetry
Jemalloc metrics are not automatically updated: you need to ask jemalloc with an epoch::advance() call. This operation is quite costly, more on this at the end. Consequently this cannot be done for each request.
We are using the OpenTelemetry SDK to export data to a metric backend (here VictoriaMetrics), with a Grafana frontend.
As the metric export interval is much higher than jemalloc advance calls (60s vs. 1s), we also need to track the minimum and maximum values during the collection interval of each metric, so we can have more insights.
First we can define a Sample struct to track the last value and the extremum of a jemalloc metric during the OTEL metric export.
Defining a sample struct to track the last measured value and its extrema
Then we can sample jemalloc metrics every second and export the results
Second step: measuring those metrics against a variable load to determine what are the most representative metrics
…
Third step: not seeing any representative metrics and asking yourself what is wrong!
Hopefully by reading this you will not fall into the same traps :D! Indeed I stumbled upon two main footguns.
Firstly, the jemallocator crate defaults to prefixed symbols, so it won’t override the malloc family of functions in the resulting binary. If you have any C dependencies like zstd for compression/decompression, it will continue to use the default libc allocator. This is a big issue because zstd’s own allocations won’t be tracked by jemalloc. Hence the usage estimation will be invalid. To circumvent this, don’t forget to enable the unprefixed_malloc_on_supported_platforms feature flag in your Cargo.toml!
Secondly, the main cause of our weird memory behavior is THP or Transparent Huge Pages!
This Linux feature might be enabled at the OS level by default. It will automatically allocate bigger pages than the ones asked by your allocator and will re-address the previously-allocated smaller pages on it. The issue is that it might increase the memory usage drastically (because a small 4 KiB allocation might be moved to a 2 MiB page) and more importantly, it won’t be tracked as resident memory by jemalloc. This only happens when the host setting is always. You can check it with cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled.
Also, even with traffic being much smaller, the RSS won’t reduce because most of it consists of huge pages.
The best solution is to disable this feature on the allocator’s memory with a madvise syscall. Jemalloc will do that for its own mappings if you specify MALLOC_CONF=thp:never. Without the unprefixed feature flag, the variable is _RJEM_MALLOC_CONF. This feature can cause a lot of other unexpected issues (see the redis doc about transparent huge page) and it only benefits certain types of workloads, so I strongly encourage you to read about it!
Jemalloc provides a lot of metrics for you: allocated, active, resident, retained, … The question is not which one matches with my RSS/memory working set measured by the OS: none will. The best we can do is to measure the evolution of each metric against the RSS and determine a formula.
This being said, if we do our measure again with these two params, we can clearly see that the most representative metric is the resident, which is no surprise. Resident memory is the closest metric to what the OS sees, because it counts allocations, allocator overhead, fragmentation and dirty pages waiting to be removed. However, check what other metrics are available from jemalloc and whether they fit your program better! Most of the time the rule will be a linear function: MAX_MEMORY = (limit - base) * factor. The base accounts for the thread stacks, the program binary and static sections. The factor is a safety margin (0.75 on the system shown below).
With a new config being rolled out with MALLOC_CONF=thp:never and unprefixed_malloc_on_supported_platforms we can see a significant RSS drop and more importantly it now follows the same shape as the resident metric!
Now let’s run a little (actually two) ingestion benchmarks to check that the resident metric follows the RSS linearly:
Here, with the two benchmarks, from 10:00 to 13:00 and from 16:00 to 17:00 we can see that resident is clearly the most appropriate metric. In comparison, the allocated metric follows the same shape but grows much less: about +30 MiB against +100 MiB for resident. The main reason is that freed memory is not released right away. It stays in dirty pages, which count as resident but not as allocated.
Fourth step: applying backpressure against the resident metric
MAX_MEMORY comes from the rule above. The 0.75 factor is there because the resident metric is a lagging signal. It is sampled every second, so memory keeps growing between two samples. The margin must absorb that growth.
It also falls slowly. Freed memory stays in dirty pages until jemalloc purges them. So the server can keep rejecting requests for a while after the load is gone.
Backpressure against resident metric
The same check works for our pull based consumer. Instead of replying a 503, it stops pulling new events while resident is above MAX_MEMORY. The stream acts as a buffer in the meantime.
A small word about jemalloc metrics performance
When calling epoch::advance() to update jemalloc metrics, it is actually going to walk every memory arena. Jemalloc has this mechanism of having multiple memory arenas in order to reduce fragmentation and lock contention. It is controllable with the narenas param and by default is set to 4 per CPU thread. As jemalloc gets the number of CPU threads with sched_getaffinity and does not follow cgroups, on a 64-core host machine, narenas will be 256, even if you have a CPU limit of 1 so make sure to verify this.
Conclusion
SolutionWhat it boundsHard bound?Main cost
IndirectRequests × max sizeYesPlanning for the worst case
Byte budgetBytes held by the tasksYesMore knobs, little crate support
GlobalThe whole heapNo, reactiveMeasuring and tuning the allocator
Indirect bounding is the easiest to set up, but you have to plan for the worst case. The global allocator solution is the easiest to operate: a single limit, and every allocation is counted. It’s the one I usually reach for in the first place. I fall back to byte-budget bounding when it fits the target system better, or when I need fine-grained control: tuning individual components separately instead of applying a single global limit. They aren’t mutually exclusive, and you can combine them if you need to. Keep in mind that the global limiter is reactive, not a hard bound. If a burst can outrun the margin, keep a concurrency limit behind it. Whichever you choose, bear in mind the performance impact on your own workload.
Let’s reclaim all the memory from LLMs!

title: Inside Serde: Building a Custom JSON Deserializer with binary support and more
body:
TL;DR
Socket.IO is a JavaScript library for real-time, bidirectional communication between clients and servers, built on top of WebSockets and featuring a custom event-based protocol.
It uses a custom packet format that doesn’t map cleanly to Rust’s type system or serde’s model — especially with variadic arguments and out-of-band binary payloads. This post walks through how I extended serde_json by wrapping its deserializer to:
Lazily extract the event name without full deserialization
Automatically reinject binary payloads into placeholders
Differentiate between tuples and vectors for correct variadic decoding
Eliminate the need for intermediate Value representation and two-phase parsing.
The result is a clean, ergonomic, and performant single-phase deserialization system — with a 10× speedup on packet routing.
Socketioxide introduction
While working on Socketioxide, an Axum-like Socket.IO server implementation in Rust, I encountered an issue I initially thought would be trivial. Spoiler: it wasn’t. It led me to rethink how serde works and ultimately dive deep into customizing it for the socketioxide needs.
The Socket.IO Protocol Quirks
Socket.IO comes with its own protocol. Under the hood, it’s mostly JSON, but with some custom rules:
The event name is encoded as the first argument of a JSON array.
It supports variadic arguments, where any number of payloads follow the event name.
Binary data isn’t inlined — instead, it’s replaced by a placeholder and sent separately (e.g., in a WebSocket binary frame).
The packet format looks something like:
For example, the following packet:
should be parsed as a binary event (packet id 5) that is part of the “/admin” namespace with 2 binary attachments. The event name is “foo” and the payload is the sequence ["message", <Buffer 01 02 ...>, <Buffer 03 04 ...>].
We want the user to be able to specify the whole spectrum of serde possibilities without being limited by socketioxide.
The final API for writing a handler with socketioxide looks like:
Serde: where it breaks down
The first emerging idea to solve this issue would be to write a custom JSON-parser that will partially decode our data. However that’s a terrible idea for many reasons.
It’s error prone, complex, the resulting code will be inefficent and insecure.
Rust and serde_json give us great tools to work with structured data, but they hit limitations in this protocol:
Tuple vs Vec ambiguity: A tuple (e.g. (i32, String)) and a vector (Vec<Value>) are both serialized to a Value::Array, making it hard to distinguish variadic arguments properly. Ideally, we’d treat tuples as argument lists, but not expand vectors.
Binary placeholders: There’s no clean way to inject binary buffers back into their correct place in the deserialized structure.
Two-phase deserialization: We must first parse the event to determine the correct handler, but the default approach fully deserializes the entire message too early, often unnecessarily.
Memory fragmentation: Using serde_json::Value for intermediate deserialization leads to lots of heap allocations.
1. Naive solution: dynamic value handling and two-phase deserialization
My first approach was to use serde_json::Value as a generic stand-in:
Extract the event name from the first element of the array.
Recursively walk the structure to locate binary placeholders and associate them with actual payloads.
Represent remaining arguments as a Vec<Value>.
Deserialize the serde_json::Value to the user provided type.
This mostly worked and had the following trade-offs:
Advantages
Simple and dynamic: Everything is handled at runtime.
No need for users to write custom serializers/deserializers.
Drawbacks
Lacks precision: Can’t distinguish tuples from vectors — a critical protocol mismatch.
No binary reinjection support: Once separated, placeholders and actual buffers are hard to correlate and rebind.
They are provided in an adjacent vector.
Value is heap-heavy: Parsing large messages fragments memory and reduces throughput.
Two-pass deserialization means doubling the amount of work.
2. Another naive solution: annotated fields
Users could put #[serde(deserialize_with = "...")] on binary fields to inject the binary buffer manually during deserialization. Unfortunately, Serde does not allow custom deserialization functions to access external state (like the binary buffer queue) in a clean way. This would also force the user to think about specifying this.
And it doesn’t solve the other issues such as the support for multiple arguments.
I wanted to stick with Serde’s ecosystem but needed more control. Thankfully serde is incredibly flexible.
The optimal solution: a custom serializer/deserializer
Hence I had three main issues:
Tuples/arrays should be used for variadics and Vec for sequences,
an issue induced by the use of an intermediate representation like serde_json::Value which makes it impossible to differentiate, as they are both represented as sequences.
Binary payload reinjection should happen at any level without iterating over an intermediate representation.
In order to get rid of the intermediate representation, the event name should be deserialized in a lazy manner without parsing the full payload up front.
Eventually, I decided to write a custom deserializer that wraps serde_json::Deserializer — this gave me:
Lazy deserialization: I can extract just the event name without parsing the full payload up front, and defer deeper parsing until we’ve routed the event.
Precise handling of tuples vs arrays: I can control how sequences are interpreted and enforce variadic behavior only where expected.
Binary buffer reinjection: I can track and inject external binary buffers at the correct locations with stateful deserialization.
Serde uses the visitor pattern for deserialization which makes it extremely modular by separating the incoming data side from the type defintion side. This pattern will be used for all the following features.
1. Lazy deserialization
Here is a quick example on how we can deserialize only the first element of a sequence by using a FirstElement struct that will be a serde visitor and a deserialize seed.
This allows us to map any kind of data to any type in a statically defined manner.
Then we can easily use our FirstElement. It’s even in a zero-copy way!
But what about deserializing the real payload? How do you skip the event name? Well, as we are wrapping the serde_json deserializer, we can implement custom behavior such as skipping the first element of the root JSON array:
We start by building a custom visitor wrapper to skip the first element in a sequence.
And we can create our visitor in our deserializer wrapper.
With this we don’t need to deserialize our data to an intermediate dynamic value, we can immediately find the corresponding event handler and deserialize the raw JSON string to a user provided type and skip the event.
2. Precise handling of tuples vs arrays for variadic arguments
In Socket.IO if you send a vec with socket.emit("event", [1, 2, 3, 4]), it will be serialized like this: [event, [1, 2, 3, 4]] but if you send variadics with socket.emit("event", 1, 2, 3, 4), it will be serialized as: [event, 1, 2, 3, 4].
But, how can we do the difference on the Rust-side? So that a multi-argument payload is deserialized to a tuple and a vector of data is deserialized to a vec?
Well, that’s the user responsibility. They will know whether they are expecting a vec or tuple!
So here is what we could do. First we need to know if the user provided a tuple or something else, prepare yourself—it’s kind of hacky.
IsTupleSerde has an implementation for serializer and deserializer that will simply error immediately with a boolean saying
if the root type appears to be a tuple or not (without visiting anything or any data):
We can then make a little function to check if a type is a tuple or not:
And then use it.
3. Binary buffer reinjection
As you saw before, with the visitor pattern we can completely separate the incoming data side with the mapped user types.
This is what we are going to do! We are going to map serde maps (the binary placeholders) to user binary types.
We can make a custom BinaryVisitor wrapper that will be instantiated for any user provided bytes types.
But with a twist! When serde_json will ask our binary visitor to visit a map, rather than bailing out, it will happily accept it and:
check that it is a placeholder, e.g.: { "_placeholder": true, "num": 1 }.
take the corresponding binary from the queue and return it.
Then we can use our BinaryVisitor wrapper for any call to deserialize_bytes or deserialize_byte_buf:
Conclusion
Et voilà! We have extended/twisted serde to do custom deserialization without writing any parsing code (I will happily let that for serde_json)!
We went from a two-phase dynamic system to a single-phase, type-safe, performant deserialization pipeline to a one-phase deserialization process that handles:
External binary data re-injection.
First element (the event name) extracted for routing and skipped for user deserialization.
Differentiation between tuples and vecs to support deserializing from JS sent variadics.
Zero-copy deserialization! Don’t get me wrong—it’s still ‘partial’ zero-copy, since we’re using JSON. But for basic strings at least.
Performance (because we all like the little thrill of perf improvements):
We reduced processing time for a basic packet from 600ns to just 60ns. Memory usage is also significantly more efficient, as no unnecessary allocations are made. Additionally, if the user chooses not to deserialize the incoming data—or if it doesn’t match the expected user types—it simply isn’t deserialized.
